clue.text: It stiffens the colourless old court

indicators.note: the court's name loses a colour, the shade of amber, so those letters drop out

parts.note: the Star Chamber was an old English court, abolished in 1641

explanation.surface: A gloomy description of a dreary, faded court of times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'colourless' takes AMBER, a colour, out of STAR CHAMBER, the notorious old English court, leaving the stiffener.
explanation.definitionFit: Laundry starch is applied to fabric to make collars and shirts rigid.

clue.text: Musketeer ordered to shoot a plant

parts.note: pictures an officer calling out to a soldier named Sam, ordering him to fire his musket

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sam, fire!' is the order given to the musketeer; said together it is the name of the coastal plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleshy coastal plant, eaten pickled or as a vegetable.

clue.text: Slough in a divine setting is highly thought of

indicators.note: the divine forms a setting round the other piece, like a mount around a jewel

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, abbreviates a divine or clergyman
a slough is a bog, also called a mire

explanation.surface: Suggests the English town of Slough looks lovely in a heavenly location.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is also a town west of London, which the surface uses; a 'divine' is a clergyman, abbreviated as a Doctor of Divinity.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone esteemed is respected and looked up to.

clue.text: All eating, drinking and being merry

definitions.text: All eating, drinking and being merry

parts.words: All eating, drinking and being merry
parts.note: describes the cheerful, sociable mood of a feast

explanation.definitionFit: Describes festive, sociable company that enjoys food, drink and fun together.

clue.text: The Order of the Bed?

parts.note: reads like a knightly order, but means both a phrase for perfect tidiness ('___ order') and a prank bed with the sheet folded short ('___ bed')

explanation.walkthrough: The same word pair goes before 'order' (neat arrangement) and before 'bed' (the schoolboy trick of folding a sheet so the sleeper cannot stretch out).
explanation.definitionFit: The dessert's name appears in two idioms: tidy arrangement order and the short-sheeted prank bed.

clue.text: Tax refunds offered by the Marshall Plan ?

explanation.surface: An official notice of tax returns linked to American postwar aid.
explanation.walkthrough: In wartime Britain extra income tax was later repaid as these credits; the Marshall Plan gave US aid to Europe after 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: Repayments of wartime extra income tax made after 1945, and literally the loans given after the war through American aid.

clue.text: But would he come off worst if he changed roles?

definitions.text: But would he come off worst if he changed roles?

indicators.note: changed shows that roles is to be rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Asks whether a person swapping roles would end up the worse for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges ROLES; the whole clue also describes the person who comes off worst.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who comes off worst is the defeated party in a contest.

clue.text: Not all in favour of one side

explanation.surface: A referee accused of bias towards one team.
explanation.definitionFit: Incomplete, and also biased or prejudiced towards one party.

clue.text: Portrait of the left inside- Figure Y

indicators.note: only the inside of the word left is used, its middle letters

parts.note: fig. is the abbreviation for figure
taken as written

explanation.surface: A caption pointing to a portrait on the left, marked as figure Y.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' takes the middle letters EF of 'left'.
explanation.definitionFit: A model or likeness of a person, often burnt in protest.

clue.text: Side door for tradesmen but not for scholars ?

definitions.text: Side door for tradesmen but not for scholars

parts.words: Side door for tradesmen but not for scholars
parts.note: a shared door used by delivery men, contrasted with the exam boys sit to get into English fee-paying schools

explanation.walkthrough: For tradesmen it is a shared door; for scholars it is the exam taken around 13 for entry to English private (public) schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a shared doorway, and also the name of the English private-school admission exam.

clue.text: Important the second round goes to us

indicators.note: goes to says the last piece is attached to follow the ones before it

parts.note: a second is a brief instant, a moment
a round shape is the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boxing commentator stresses that the second round has gone to us.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something of great consequence is significant and weighty.

clue.text: Sometimes a capital feature backfires

indicators.note: back, joined to the word it turns, says the word fires is read in reverse

parts.note: the clue word is split into back plus fires, so the letters sit at its end by the split, a coincidence of the word, not a hidden-word device

explanation.surface: A warning that a plan in the capital city sometimes goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' in 'backfires' reverses FIRES. A capital here is a capital letter, which in many typefaces carries small finishing strokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the small cross-strokes at the ends of letters, found on capitals in typefaces like Times.

clue.text: Virtue not apparent to one's valet

definitions.text: Virtue not apparent to one's valet

parts.words: Virtue not apparent to one's valet
parts.note: alludes to the saying that no man is a great figure to his own valet, who sees him at his most ordinary

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'No man is a hero to his valet' supplies the virtue a servant never sees.
explanation.definitionFit: Courage and greatness are the qualities a personal servant, seeing his master daily, fails to notice.

clue.text: Is Labour such a party ?

parts.note: the Labour Party is named for the workers; a committee set up to study a problem has the same name with 'party'

explanation.walkthrough: A committee set up to investigate is a '___ party'; Labour, Britain's left-wing party, was founded for the labouring class.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour means toil, and a toiling group studying a question is a ___ party.

clue.text: Bones in a circle

explanation.surface: An archaeologist finds bones laid out in a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of the forearm bone's name, and also of the lines from the centre to the rim of a round figure.

clue.text: No smoke without bubble here

parts.note: plays on 'no smoke without fire': this oriental pipe draws smoke through water, so every puff bubbles

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'no smoke without fire' is turned: a water pipe (hookah) cannot be smoked without bubbling.
explanation.definitionFit: A hookah, the oriental tobacco pipe whose smoke is cooled by passing through a water bowl.

clue.text: What the jet set use for smoking old socks'?

definitions.text: What the jet set use for smoking old socks

parts.words: What the jet set use for smoking old socks
parts.note: old socks are hose; the jet set are people with water jets, and smoking suggests pipes

explanation.walkthrough: Hose is an old word for socks or stockings, so 'pipes' for hose sound like smoking pipes; the jet is a water jet from a garden tube.
explanation.definitionFit: Flexible tubes for sending a jet of water, as in a garden.

clue.text: Concluded that the finer variety needs colour

indicators.note: a variety of finer is a different arrangement of its letters

parts.note: red is a colour

explanation.surface: Decided that the better strain of a plant needs some colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' rearranges FINER into INFER.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: deduced from evidence.

clue.text: Modern transport causing rail trouble in the East ? Right !

indicators.note: rail in trouble is thrown into disorder, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A report of railway disruption in eastern parts, with a cheer at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures railway trouble; the rail letters are rearranged, and 'in the East' gives two pieces, the word itself and the compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: A passenger aircraft is a current means of travel, newer than the railway.

clue.text: Suggesting that the Bard is not well disposed to us ?

definitions.text: Suggesting that the Bard is not well disposed to us

parts.words: Suggesting that the Bard is not well disposed to us
parts.note: the Bard is Shakespeare, Will; not well means sick, and the phrase also means hostile feeling

explanation.walkthrough: The Bard, Shakespeare, is Will; read the phrase as 'sick Will', or as hostility towards us.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostility or animosity, here also read as Shakespeare being unwell.

clue.text: She gives us a new part

indicators.note: only part of the words gives us a new is used, a run of consecutive letters

explanation.surface: An actress is given a fresh role by the director.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' points to a run hidden inside 'giveS US A New'. The surface makes 'part' a stage role.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so it can stand for a female 'she'.

clue.text: What's the point in chasing Jack up here ?

definitions.text: What's the point in chasing Jack up here

parts.words: What's the point in chasing Jack up here
parts.note: point means a spire; chasing and jack each go with this word, as a horse race and a man who climbs tall towers

explanation.walkthrough: The word combines with 'chasing' (a horse race over jumps) and 'jack' (a worker who climbs tall towers), and is a church's pointed spire.
explanation.definitionFit: A church tower topped with a pointed spire.

clue.text: Jack and Bill have us down for the count

indicators.note: in a down entry, the next piece is placed below the others

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, abbreviated AB for able seaman
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC

explanation.surface: A boxing match where Jack and Bill floor us for a count of ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down' puts US beneath AB and AC; the boxing image of being 'down for the count' misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: A frame of sliding beads used for doing arithmetic.

clue.text: Capital support on retirement

parts.note: capital is read as the head and retirement as going to bed, not a pension fund

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a pension investment; read 'capital' as the head (Latin caput) and 'retirement' as going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A long firm pillow placed under the head when lying down in bed.

clue.text: Drum Mountain

explanation.definitionFit: A small medieval drum, and a mountain in Galilee in Israel.

clue.text: Empty the unruly deep without obstruction

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the rearranged letters surround the other piece
deep behaving unruly is out of order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: in tennis a let is a ball obstructed by the net, and let also means hindrance

explanation.surface: A command to drain a rough sea with nothing to block it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, and 'let' is an old word for hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to drain or use up a supply until little is left.

clue.text: Get up or (if worsted) down

parts.note: the verb means to rise; add 'down' and it means to back off after being beaten (worsted)

explanation.walkthrough: 'Worsted' here means beaten, not the wool: a beaten person backs out, does a '___ down'.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend, and with 'down' added, to retreat from a position after defeat.

clue.text: It's for men of letters rather than composers and money-makers

definitions.text: It's for men of letters rather than composers and money-makers

parts.words: It's for men of letters rather than composers and money-makers
parts.note: men of letters are writers of correspondence; composers write musical notes and money-makers print paper money

explanation.walkthrough: Composers deal in notes and banks issue paper money, but the compound is writing paper for letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stationery sheets used for writing letters.

clue.text: B.B.C.'s overheads when a serial's involved

indicators.note: involved means tangled or complicated, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A grumble that the broadcaster's costs rise whenever it makes a drama series.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges A SERIALS, the S of the 's counting as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Staff pay is the main running cost of an organisation such as the BBC, Britain's public broadcaster.

clue.text: 26 sounds like the donkey's tail

indicators.note: says the word said aloud resembles the spoken phrase

parts.note: a donkey is an ass, and its tail is at its rear end

explanation.surface: A remark on what a donkey's tail resembles in noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is CLIMB, the answer to 26-across. 'Ass end', the donkey's back end, said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym of the answer to 26: to go up.
